title: Unmasking the Duo: Wilson's Disease in the Context of Lupus and Existing Hepatitis E Coinfection
case_prompt:
An 18-year-old woman presented in September 2024 with a 1-month history of low-grade intermittent fever accompanied by rigors, chills, myalgias, and arthralgias, followed 20 days later by scleral icterus that progressed to generalized jaundice with a purplish rash and dark urine. She then developed bizarre behavior, an initial mutism, and later irrelevant speech, while remaining conscious. Over the preceding 18 months, she had experienced oral ulcers, alopecia, and arthralgias of the small joints of the hands and feet without swelling or stiffness, as well as exertional dyspnea and palpitations for 1 year. There was no history of sore throat, cough, gastrointestinal bleeding, or medication use prior to these symptoms. Her parents were consanguineous; her father had a long‐standing psychiatric illness.

On examination, she was febrile (102°F), disoriented to time and place, mildly jaundiced, and pale, with facial puffiness, bilateral nontender parotid enlargement, angular cheilitis, and livedo reticularis with necrotic plaques on the skin. Neurologically, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13, with no focal deficits, no meningeal signs, and no Kayser–Fleischer rings. The abdomen showed mild splenomegaly.  

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, leukocytes 2.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 40 × 10^9/L), AST 1292 U/L, total bilirubin 11.5 mg/dL, and a reversed albumin:globulin ratio. Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative; hepatitis E IgM was positive. Ceruloplasmin was low (0.2 g/L), and 24-hour urinary copper excretion was elevated (204 µg). Autoimmune testing showed a positive ANA (coarse speckled pattern), high anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro, anti-La, U1-RNP, rheumatoid factor, anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, a positive direct Coombs test, and low complement levels.  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatosplenomegaly, increased hepatic echogenicity, and a small amount of perihepatic fluid. MRI of the brain with contrast, MRA, and MRV showed dilated ventricles with minimal subependymal seepage, mucoperiosteal thickening of the sphenoid sinus, and a normal appearance of the basal ganglia; the remainder of the studies were unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Systemic lupus erythematosus was considered because of mucocutaneous signs, arthralgias, and positive serologies — “the presence of mucocutaneous and joint symptoms ... was confirmed by a positive workup for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).”  
2. Acute hepatitis E infection was included to explain the jaundice — “Her jaundice could be explained by simultaneous acute Hepatitis E infection, as indicated by a positive hepatitis E IgM antibody.”  
3. Drug-induced lupus was considered in the context of WD therapy but excluded here — “treatment of WD with penicillamine ... has been associated with drug-induced lupus,” yet “the patient had not taken any medication for Wilson's and particularly not penicillamine.”  
4. Autoimmune hepatitis was a potential secondary cause of liver involvement in SLE — “secondary causes include viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and drug-induced liver injury.”  
5. Lupus cerebritis was in the differential for neuropsychiatric symptoms in SLE — “neuropsychiatric disturbances such as loss of speech and emotional lability” could represent CNS lupus.  
6. Wilson’s disease was suspected based on neuropsychiatric features, family history, and consanguinity — “the presence of neuropsychiatric symptoms along with a longstanding family history of psychiatric illness in her father and her being a product of a consanguineous marriage raised further suspicion of an inherited metabolic disorder.”
